sections.body_md:
Open-loop control computes a command from the reference and a model, then sends it. A valve, a heater, or a motor voltage is chosen ahead of time. If the plant matches the model and nothing else pushes on the output, the result is right. Real plants drift. Loads, grade, and supply changes show up one-for-one at the output, because nothing is watching that output.

Closed-loop control measures the output, subtracts the measurement from the reference, and lets the controller act on the error. The plant is the thing being controlled. The actuator turns the command into a physical cause. The sensor reports the output. The reference is the desired output. A disturbance is an unwanted input, at the actuator or at the output. Sensor noise is a false piece of the measurement.

The loop can reject disturbances and make the output less sensitive to plant changes. The price is that the loop can oscillate, and sensor noise is driven into the command. Those tradeoffs are why feedback is designed, not just switched on.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Open loop, with a command \(u\) chosen from the reference,
\[ y = P u + d. \]
If the model says the plant gain is \(P_\mathrm{model}\), the usual command is \(u = r/P_\mathrm{model}\). The true output is then \((P/P_\mathrm{model}) r + d\).

Closed loop with the proportional law \(u = K_c(r-y)\) and the same output disturbance,
\[ y = \frac{L}{1+L} r + \frac{1}{1+L} d, \qquad L = K_c P. \]
The tracking factor \(T = L/(1+L)\) multiplies the reference and the sensor noise. The sensitivity \(S = 1/(1+L)\) multiplies an output disturbance and, approximately, a fractional plant change. Large \(L\) makes \(T\) near \(1\) and \(S\) near \(0\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A flow plant is modeled as \(7\ \mathrm{L/min}\) per volt. The reference is \(14\ \mathrm{L/min}\), so the open-loop command is \(2\ \mathrm{V}\). If the true gain is \(9\ \mathrm{L/min}\) per volt, the flow is \(18\ \mathrm{L/min}\), which is \(4\ \mathrm{L/min}\) above the reference.

Close the loop with \(K_c = 3\ \mathrm{V}\) per \((\mathrm{L/min})\). On the model gain the loop gain is \(21\), and the flow is \(13.36\ \mathrm{L/min}\). An extra \(4.4\ \mathrm{L/min}\) of output disturbance contributes only \(0.20\ \mathrm{L/min}\). With the true gain \(9\), the loop gain is \(27\) and the flow is \(13.50\ \mathrm{L/min}\), still near the reference of \(14\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Treating a calibrated open-loop command as if it rejected disturbances.
- Swapping \(S\) and \(T\). Disturbances and plant changes see \(S\). The reference and sensor noise see \(T\).
- Forgetting that the actuator and the sensor are real blocks, with their own limits.
- Adding the measurement instead of subtracting it. The denominator becomes \(1-L\), and a large loop gain makes the loop run away.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Block-diagram algebra collapses series and feedback pictures to one gain. On-off and proportional laws are the first controllers that close the loop. A vehicle speed loop is the same picture, with drag as the plant and grade as the disturbance.
